The LAMBADA dataset: Word prediction requiring a broad discourse context. In Proceedings of the 54th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, pages 1525–1534, Berlin, Germany.
creator: Denis Paperno, Germán Kruszewski, Angeliki Lazaridou, Quan Ngoc Pham, Raffaella Bernardi, Sandro Pezzelle, Marco Baroni, Gemma Boleda, Raquel Fernández (CIMeC - Center for Mind/Brain Sciences, University of Trento; Institute for Logic, Language & Computation, University of Amsterdam)
description: LAMBADA (LAnguage Modeling Broadened to Account for Discourse Aspects) is a collection of narrative passages where the task is to predict the last word of a target sentence. The passages are selected such that human subjects can guess the target word when given the full passage (broad context), but not when given only the last sentence. It consists of 10,022 passages divided into 4,869 development and 5,153 test passages, drawn from the BookCorpus.
name: LAMBADA
publisher: CIMeC - Center for Mind/Brain Sciences, University of Trento
rai:annotationsPerItem: At least 2 subjects confirmed guessability from full passage (steps 1 and 2), plus up to 10 subjects attempted guessing from sentence only (step 3).
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: In the crowdsourcing pipeline, 84–86% of items were discarded at step 1, an additional 6–7% at step 2, and another 3–5% at step 3. Only about one in 25 input examples passed all selection steps. The strict hit-or-miss approach required two consecutive subjects to exactly match the missing word, and no subject (out of ten) to provide it based on local context only.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Three-step crowdsourcing pipeline: (1) one subject guessed the target word from the full passage; if correct, (2) a second subject guessed from the full passage; if also correct, (3) up to 10 subjects tried to guess from the target sentence only (3 guesses per sentence allowed). A passage was included in LAMBADA only if no subject in step 3 could guess the target word. Subjects in steps 1 and 2 were paid $0.22 per page (10 passages/page); step 3 subjects were paid $0.15 per page (20 sentences/page). The same subject could not judge the same item in both passage and sentence conditions.
rai:dataBiases: LAMBADA is heavily skewed toward proper nouns as target words (48%), which are hugely over-represented compared to the input data distribution. The dataset also contains quoted direct speech significantly more often than the input items (71% vs. 61%). The use of unpublished novels from BookCorpus was a deliberate design choice to minimize the usefulness of general world knowledge and external resources.
rai:dataCollection: Passages were drawn from the BookCorpus (unpublished novels). Candidate passages were first filtered by automated language models to remove easy-to-guess items, then evaluated by human subjects via CrowdFlower crowdsourcing in a three-step pipeline: (1) one subject guessed the target word from the full passage; (2) a second subject guessed from the full passage; (3) multiple subjects tried to guess from the target sentence only (up to 10 unsuccessful guesses). Only passages passing all three steps were included.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw source data is the BookCorpus (Zhu et al., 2015), a collection of 5,325 novels and 465 million words (after duplicate removal and filtering of potentially offensive material). The corpus contains unpublished novels.
rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Web Scraping, Manual Human Curator
rai:dataLimitations: LAMBADA is designed as a challenging test set where standard language models are bound to fail by design (one of the first filters was to choose passages where simple language models failed). The dataset is skewed toward proper nouns and narrative/dialogue text from novels. The strict hit-or-miss annotation approach may exclude valid synonymous or paraphrastic answers. Cost considerations precluded using more subjects at stage 1, which could in principle improve filtering quality.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The BookCorpus was preprocessed by removing duplicates and filtering potentially offensive material using a stop word list. Novels were randomly divided into training and development+testing partitions. Candidate passages were filtered using a combination of four language models (a pre-trained RNN and three models trained on BookCorpus: a 4-gram model, an RNN, and a feed-forward model); any passage whose target word had probability ≥0.00175 according to any model was excluded.
rai:dataSocialImpact: LAMBADA is intended to advance research in natural language understanding by providing a benchmark that requires genuine broad-context comprehension, going beyond statistical pattern matching. The authors believe that leveraging human performance on word prediction is a promising strategy to construct benchmarks for computational models that capture various aspects of human text understanding.
rai:dataUseCases: LAMBADA is intended as a challenging benchmark to evaluate computational models' ability to understand broad discourse context in natural language text, specifically for word prediction tasks. It is proposed as a test set to encourage development of new models capable of genuine understanding of broad context. The authors also plan to use it as the basis for a public competition.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Four language models were used to pre-filter passages: a pre-trained RNN (Mikolov et al., 2011) and three models trained on BookCorpus (a standard 4-gram model, an RNN, and a feed-forward neural network model). Any passage whose target word had probability ≥0.00175 according to any model was excluded.

evidence.name: We introduce LAMBADA, a dataset to evaluate the capabilities of computational models for text understanding by means of a word prediction task.
evidence.description: LAMBADA is a collection of narrative passages sharing the characteristic that human subjects are able to guess their last word if they are exposed to the whole passage, but not if they only see the last sentence preceding the target word. To succeed on LAMBADA, computational models cannot simply rely on local context, but must be able to keep track of information in the broader discourse.

evidence.inLanguage: LAMBADA proposes a word prediction task where the target item is difficult to guess (for English speakers) when only the sentence in which it appears is available, but becomes easy when a broader context is presented.

evidence.isLiveDataset: The LAMBADA dataset consists of 10,022 passages, divided into 4,869 development and 5,153 test passages (extracted from 1,331 and 1,332 disjoint novels, respectively).

evidence.rai:dataCollectionType: The LAMBADA data come from the Book Corpus (Zhu et al., 2015). The fact that it contains unpublished novels minimizes the potential usefulness of general world knowledge and external resources for the task.
evidence.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The corpus, after duplicate removal and filtering out of potentially offensive material with a stop word list, contains 5,325 novels and 465 million words. We randomly divided the novels into equally-sized training and development+testing partitions.
evidence.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: We used a combination of four language models, chosen by availability and/or ease of training: a pre-trained recurrent neural network (RNN) (Mikolov et al., 2011) and three models trained on the Book Corpus (a standard 4-gram model, a RNN and a feed-forward model; see SM for details). Any passage whose target word had probability ≥0.00175 according to any of the language models was excluded.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: A random sample of the remaining passages were then evaluated by human subjects through the CrowdFlower crowdsourcing service
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Subjects were paid $0.22 per page in steps 1 and 2 (with 10 passages per page) and $0.15 per page in step 3 (with 20 sentences per page). Overall, each item in the resulting dataset costed $1.24 on average. We made sure that it was not possible for the same subject to judge the same item in both passage and sentence conditions.
evidence.rai:annotationsPerItem: more subjects tried to guess the target word based on the target sentence only, until the word was guessed or the number of unsuccessful guesses reached 10; if no subject was able to guess the target word, the passage was added to the LAMBADA dataset.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: In the crowdsourcing pipeline, 84–86% items were discarded at step 1, an additional 6–7% at step 2 and another 3–5% at step 3. Only about one in 25 input examples passed all the selection steps.
evidence.rai:dataBiases: Figure 2(b) shows that most target words in LAMBADA are proper nouns (48%), followed by common nouns (37%) and, at a distance, verbs (7.7%). In fact, proper nouns are hugely over-represented in LAMBADA, while the other categories are under-represented, compared to the POS distribution in the input.
evidence.rai:dataLimitations: We also note that, because of the way we have constructed LAMBADA, standard language models are bound to fail on it by design: one of our first filters (see Section 3.1) was to choose passages where a number of simple language models were failing to predict the upcoming word.
evidence.rai:dataUseCases: We thus propose LAMBADA as a challenging test set, meant to encourage the development of new models capable of genuine understanding of broad context in natural language text. We plan to announce a public competition based on the LAMBADA data.
evidence.rai:dataSocialImpact: We believe that leveraging human performance on word prediction is a very promising strategy to construct benchmarks for computational models that are supposed to capture various aspects of human text understanding. The influence of broad context as explored by LAMBADA is only one example of this idea.

Any passage whose target word had probability ≥0.00175 according to any of the language models was excluded.
